extracted.intended_audience: political science researchers, policy analysts, and data scientists studying public comments, lobbying coalitions, and mobilization in federal rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying, classifying, and measuring public pressure (mass comment) campaigns in federal rulemaking using text-reuse, hand-coding, and coalition-based approaches; testing hypotheses about who mobilizes, when, and with what effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis: Most engagement results from organized public pressure campaigns (Hypothesis 2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most people engage in the policy process due to organized public pressure campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical expectation: the majority of comments on regulations.gov will be part of mass comment campaigns. Figure 2.11 indicates that since 2007 the vast majority of comments each year were the result of a public pressure campaign. Use shading/counts of comments classified as part of campaigns vs not to evaluate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who launches campaigns: public vs private interest prevalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether most public pressure campaigns are launched by public interest groups in absolute terms, or whether public interest groups are more likely to use public pressure campaigns when they lobby than private interests are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare frequency of campaigns initiated by groups coded as public-interest-driven coalitions versus private-interest-driven coalitions. This is both an absolute-count test (who launches most campaigns) and a conditional-rate test (probability a lobbying coalition uses mobilization given they lobby).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis: Public-interest coalitions elicit larger responses to mobilizing efforts (Hypothesis 2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public interest group coalitions have a larger response to their mobilizing efforts than private interest group (e.g., business-led) coalitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize 'response' as number/scale of comments mobilized per unit of mobilization effort (e.g., spending, solicitations). Behavioral intuition: individuals are more easily mobilized to sign a form letter from a public interest group than from a private interest group. Compare response curves or people-per-dollar (or per-solicitation) across coalition types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource/capacity requirement for mobilization (Hypothesis 2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mobilizing people for national policy rulemaking requires significant organizing capacity; most public pressure campaigns targeting national policy are run by large national policy advocacy organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect campaigns to be concentrated among organizations with the resources and infrastructure to run mass mobilizations (policy advocacy organizations vs small membership groups). Evidence: identify lead organizations and measure organizational size/capacity when attributing campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reactive mobilization by private interests (Hypothesis 2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If narrow private interest groups (e.g., businesses) launch public pressure campaigns, it is often a response to an opposing campaign; private interest groups will rarely lobby unopposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test by measuring how often private-interest-led coalitions lobby alone versus alongside/opposed to other coalitions. Evidence supporting Hypothesis 2.6: public interest group coalitions more often lobby unopposed than private interest groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of analysis: lobbying coalitions (coalition-level measurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary unit of analysis is the lobbying coalition — a group of organizations advocating for the same policy changes on a docket — rather than the individual organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: organizations often form coalitions and both mobilize and submit technical comments; counting at the organization level can overcount a single coalition's campaign as many smaller campaigns. Measure comments per coalition and identify lead organizations; avoid treating coalition partners as independent campaigns when they are part of the same coordinated effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text-reuse identification: 10-word n-gram overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify clusters of similar comments using textual similarity by computing percent of words shared using a 10-word (10-gram) moving window across comment pairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation notes: loop over comment pairs to identify matches of 10-grams; identical documents show 100% overlap; partial matches indicate coalitions or shared templates. Use percent-shared-text matrices (example shown in Figure 2.9). Account for OCR/header/footer noise in hand-written OCRed comments. Tengrams appearing in 100+ comments indicate a mass comment campaign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thresholds for mass comment campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational thresholds for identifying mass comment campaigns: tengrams that appear in 100 or more comments indicate a mass comment campaign; clusters of 100 or more similar comments warrant hand-coding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sampling strategy uses these thresholds: one hand-coded sample contains at least one comment from each cluster (coalition) of 100 or more similar comments. The corpus identification captures organizations responsible for mobilizing 100+ comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hand-coded sampling strategy for validation and coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use several hand-coded samples: (1) a census sample that contains at least one comment from each cluster of 100+ similar comments; (2) nearly all comments on a random sample of rules; (3) nearly all comments on another random sample weighted by number of comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: permit valid observations about public pressure campaigns across agencies and over time, and allow inference about coalitions that do and do not use mass campaigns. Use iterative hand-coding to build a corpus of known organizations for computational matching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linking comments to organizations and coalitions (iterative regex + human coding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the organization responsible for each comment by searching comment text and metadata using regular expressions, building a corpus of known organization names, and iteratively validating with human coders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With research assistants, inspect samples, link names, and expand the list of organizations; include organizations responsible for over 40 million comments, covering all organizations mobilizing 100+ comments. Use the growing corpus to improve automated matching in subsequent passes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifying coalitions as public-interest or private-interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Code each coalition as primarily advancing an idea of the public interest (public-interest coalition) or more narrow private interests (private-interest coalition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heuristic rules: public interest coalitions are almost always non-profits and governments; private interest coalitions tend to be companies and industry associations. For hard cases (e.g., unions), classify based on coalition partners: if a union lobbies alongside businesses -> private-interest coalition; if it lobbies with public interest groups on public health/safety -> public-interest coalition. Consider who leads or organizes the coalition (lead organization) and whether the coalition's asks are compatible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding policy positions via spatial coding (support vs opposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place each commenter on a spatial scale relative to change between the status quo (x1) and the proposed rule (x2); code commenter i's ideal point p_i and determine support or opposition by whether p_i is closer to x2 (support) or x1 (oppose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle nuances: commenters may oppose because the proposal moves in the wrong direction (p_i < x1), or oppose because the proposal moves insufficiently toward their preferred point (e.g., prefer x3 > x2). Code statements indicating 'stronger, not weaker' as opposition to movement in wrong direction; 'applaud but prefer less severe limits' as conditional support. Assign coalition position as lead organization's position; for robustness also compute coalition average position. Divergent asks count as different coalitions unless compatible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assigning coalition membership and position
rubrics_metrics.description: When organizations submit comments together or use identical/shared text, treat them as members of the same coalition; assign the coalition's position as the lead organization's position (or average as robustness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If organizations use identical wording or text-reuse, interpret that as endorsing the same policy position as part of a lobbying coalition. If coalition members have nearly identical positions, treat as single coalition; if members have incompatible asks, treat as separate coalitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling deduplication and representative comments
rubrics_metrics.description: When agencies de-duplicate comments and provide a representative sample comment, assume the example comment is representative and link other comments to the sample based on that text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that some agencies' de-duping software will provide only a representative sample; the method assumes representativeness and links accordingly. Be cautious: deduping may mask the true number of identical submissions, so interpret counts with awareness of agency preprocessing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators and coding rules for astroturf (spectrum of grassroots↔astroturf)
rubrics_metrics.description: Astroturf campaigns are characterized by paid or deceptive mobilization to create an appearance of public support (e.g., paid petition gatherers, misleading solicitations, fake or non-consenting signatories, duplicate signatures, paid actors at events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observable indicators: identical form letters, lack of transparency about who organized or paid for signatures, duplicate submissions (same signatures across submissions), organizations collecting signatures with no plausible base of supporters, evidence of payments or subcontracted solicitors, photo evidence of paid staff handing out swag for signatures. Examples: API/Energy Citizens (bussed/paid actors, duplicate submissions), Axcess Financial (storefront solicitation, paid uploads, church solicitations, paid community organizations), Joe Jansen USB submissions. Nuanced cases: campaigns where sponsor is transparent and signers plausibly have genuine interest (e.g., Shell's template signed largely by industry workers) are coded as non-astroturf.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring mobilization success and public support moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Scale and intensity of public engagement depend on preexisting public support for the proposition being solicited; broader public-interest coalitions should mobilize more people for a given level of mobilization effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize by comparing numbers mobilized per unit of effort (spending, solicitations). Expect public-interest coalitions to have higher people-per-effort due to broader latent support; compare across coalition types and control for organizational capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing grassroots vs astroturf on a spectrum
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterize campaigns along a continuum from grassroots (driven by volunteerism and supportive public segments, often organized by policy advocacy orgs) to astroturf (paid, deceptive, or primarily appearance-driven mobilization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features of grassroots: mobilization by advocacy organizations with mailing lists/media operations, volunteers, transparent ties to organizers. Features of astroturf: paid mobilizers, deception, lack of transparency, signatures unlikely to reflect genuine underlying interest. Use qualitative evidence (e.g., websites, social media, photos, disclosures) and the pattern of submissions to place campaigns on the spectrum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding organizational-level overcounting (count coalitions, not organizations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not count each organization in a large coalition as an independent 'campaign' when the coalition runs a single coordinated campaign; measure at coalition level to avoid non-independence and inflation of campaign counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: treating one coalition's campaign as 40 smaller campaigns distorts analysis. Previous work that counts organization-level campaigns may overestimate number of distinct campaigns; use text-reuse and coalition-linking to collapse organizational submissions into coalition-level campaigns.
